view.stem: Which statements about ordinary specular reflection of light at a smooth mirror surface are correct? The normal always means the local normal at the point of incidence; nonnormal incidence means that the incident ray does not lie along the normal.

options.text: At nonnormal incidence, the incident ray, reflected ray, and normal are coplanar, and the two rays lie on opposite sides of the normal.
The angles of incidence and reflection should be defined as the angles that the incident and reflected rays, respectively, make with the tangent plane at the point of incidence.
At nonnormal incidence, the incident and reflected rays are coplanar, and both rays lie on the same side of the normal.
The angles of incidence and reflection are each measured from the normal at the point of incidence, and the two angles are equal.
At nonnormal incidence, the plane defined by the incident ray and normal is perpendicular to the plane defined by the reflected ray and normal.
At normal incidence, both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are zero, and the reflected ray retraces the original straight line.

intent.task: Judge together the complete reflection law: coplanarity, angles measured from the local normal, equal angles, and the side relationship at nonnormal incidence, including the degenerate special case of normal incidence.
intent.source_solution: The complete independent source solution was frozen before the option file was constructed. In ordinary specular reflection, the incident ray, reflected ray, and local normal at the point of incidence are coplanar; at nonnormal incidence, the two rays lie on opposite sides of the normal. Both angles are measured from the normal and are equal. At normal incidence, both angles are zero, and the reflected ray retraces the incident straight line in the opposite direction; the plane of incidence is then not unique, but coplanarity can still be satisfied. Resolving the incident propagation direction into normal and tangential components, reflection preserves the tangential component and reverses the normal component. The resulting direction lies in the plane spanned by the incident direction and normal, and the two geometric ray branches make equal angles with the normal. Their complementary angles with the tangent plane are also equal, but these are not the standard named definitions of the angles of incidence and reflection.
intent.unit_reason: The original task asks for a statement of a complete law containing several joint constraints. One native multiple unit judges the conditions and the special case of normal incidence together, avoiding fragmented true-or-false questions for individual definitions. The six candidate statements represent correct conditions and three specific erroneous procedures; the question count is not determined by the number of definitions or a question quota.
limitations: Selecting correct statements cannot demonstrate unaided oral or written recall, or the ability to explain the reflection law completely without options.
The scope is ordinary geometrical-optics specular reflection; no tasks about material reflectivity, light amplitude, or refraction are added.
No corresponding whitelisted definition prose is present. The complete independent conceptual source question is used legitimately; a worked ray-diagram example is not supplemented into a definition.

rationales.derivation: Reflection preserves the tangential component of the incident propagation direction and reverses its normal component, so the incident and reflected directions lie in the same plane defined by the incident direction and normal. Treating rays as geometric branches extending from the point of incidence toward the source and toward the reflected side, the two branches lie on opposite sides of the normal at nonnormal incidence.

The standard angles of incidence and reflection are measured between the respective rays and the local normal. The angles between the rays and tangent plane are their complements; equal complementary angles can be an equivalent geometric description, but do not redefine the standard angles as measured from the tangent plane.
rationales.misconception: First use the tangent plane as an easily constructed reference, then replace the normal-based angle by the ray-to-tangent-plane angle and incorrectly name this complementary angle the angle of incidence or reflection.

rationales.derivation: At nonnormal incidence, the incident and reflected ray branches are symmetric about the normal in the plane of incidence and lie on opposite sides of it. Coplanarity does not change this opposite-side relationship to a same-side relationship.
rationales.misconception: Retain only coplanarity, copy the incident branch directed from the point of incidence toward the source onto the same side of the normal as the reflected branch, and omit reflection symmetry about the normal, obtaining two rays on the same side.

rationales.derivation: The standard reference for both angles is the local normal at the point of incidence. Reflection reverses the sign of the normal component without changing its magnitude and leaves the tangential component unchanged, so the two geometric ray branches make equal acute angles with the normal; at normal incidence, both angles are zero.
At nonnormal incidence, the plane of incidence defined by the incident ray and normal is also the plane containing the reflected ray, not another plane perpendicular to it.
rationales.misconception: First find the plane containing the incident ray and normal, then preserve the angle to the normal while rotating the reflected ray a quarter-turn about the normal, mistakenly assuming that equal angles alone permit a perpendicular plane.

rationales.derivation: At normal incidence, the incident direction lies along the normal and its tangential component is zero. Reflection reverses the normal propagation direction without creating a tangential component, so the ray retraces the original straight line and both angles are zero.

view.stem: In the paraxial approximation, which statement correctly describes the principal foci of concave and convex mirrors? In front of the mirror means the side containing the incident light.

options.text: After reflection of rays parallel to the principal axis, the concave mirror has a virtual principal focus behind the mirror where the backward extensions meet; the convex mirror has a real principal focus in front of the mirror where the reflected rays intersect.

After reflection of rays parallel to the principal axis, the concave mirror has a real principal focus in front of the mirror where the reflected rays intersect; the convex mirror has a real principal focus behind the mirror where the reflected rays actually intersect.

After reflection of rays parallel to the principal axis, the concave mirror has a real principal focus in front of the mirror where the reflected rays intersect; the convex mirror has a virtual principal focus behind the mirror where the backward extensions meet.

After reflection of rays parallel to the principal axis, the concave mirror has a real principal focus at the center of curvature in front of the mirror where the reflected rays intersect; the convex mirror has a virtual principal focus at the center of curvature behind the mirror where the backward extensions meet.

intent.task: Recognize the complete definition of a spherical mirror principal focus, preserving parallel incidence along the principal axis, the paraxial approximation, the concave/convex distinction, and the distinction between actual reflected rays and backward extensions.
intent.source_solution: The source solution frozen before the options: in the paraxial model, the principal focus is the position on the principal axis where the reflected rays, or their backward extensions, converge after incidence close and parallel to that axis. A concave mirror has actual reflected-ray intersection on the incident side, so its principal focus in front of the mirror is real. A convex mirror has reflected rays that diverge on the incident side; their backward extensions intersect behind the mirror, so its principal focus is virtual. Actual reflected rays do not pass through the virtual focus behind the mirror. For small height y, the normal tilt is approximately y/R and the reflected direction changes by approximately 2y/R, so the focal-distance magnitude in the first-order paraxial model is R/2 rather than the center-of-curvature distance R. An arbitrarily wide spherical-mirror beam cannot be claimed to converge exactly at one point; the question does not extend to that case.
intent.unit_reason: The original principal-focus definition jointly covers both curvatures and the distinction between real light paths and virtual extensions. One native single unit compares complete concave/convex pairings and preserves their coupled distinction; separate true-or-false questions are not created for each mirror or property. This is an independent concept distinct from the reflection-law source question; the two source tasks together correspond to two response units.
limitations: Recognizing the definition cannot demonstrate unaided complete recall of the principal focus, concave/convex differences, or real/virtual properties.
The focus is described only in the explicit paraxial model; exact convergence of arbitrarily wide beams is not claimed, and unknown source-figure curvatures or numbers are not supplied.
The internal R/2 derivation is independent mathematical verification, not a source-figure measurement or an additional numerical problem presented to learners.
The lesson ray-diagram worked example or the old Q3 draft is not cited as a definition.

rationales.derivation: A concave mirror reflects near-axis rays parallel to the principal axis into convergence in front of the mirror; a convex mirror makes them diverge, with only their extensions intersecting behind the mirror. This option interchanges the convergence and divergence behavior of the two mirrors.
rationales.misconception: First exchange the deflection directions of concave and convex surfaces for parallel light, then classify extension intersections as virtual and actual converging intersections as real, obtaining the reversed complete pairing.

rationales.derivation: A convex mirror's actual reflected rays diverge in front of the mirror rather than actually intersecting behind it; the intersection behind the mirror belongs to backward extensions and is therefore virtual. The correct concave-mirror part does not make the entire definition correct.
rationales.misconception: Treat the backward-extended portions of convex-mirror reflected rays as actual light paths, then use the presence of an intersection as proof of real convergence and rename the virtual focus a real focus.

rationales.derivation: A concave mirror's local normals reflect near-axis parallel light toward the principal axis, producing actual convergence on the incident side and a real principal focus. A convex mirror's reflected rays diverge, while their backward extensions converge on the principal axis behind the mirror, producing a virtual principal focus; both use the paraxial approximation stated in the stem.

The center of curvature lies along extended local normals to the spherical surface, but is not the principal focus of rays incident parallel to the principal axis. Small-angle reflection doubles the effect of the normal tilt, giving a paraxial focal-distance magnitude R/2 rather than the center-of-curvature distance R.
rationales.misconception: Incorrectly apply the fact that all spherical-surface normals pass through the center of curvature to rays reflected after axis-parallel incidence. Use the intersection of the normals directly as the principal focus, ignoring the doubled deflection from reflection.

view.stem: In a paraxial concave-mirror imaging model, consider rays from the same off-axis object point. All incident rays discussed here lie within the paraxial range and actually strike the mirror's reflecting surface. Which incident-to-reflected-ray correspondences are correct?

options.text: An incident ray passing through the focus is reflected parallel to the principal axis.
An incident ray passing through the center of curvature is reflected parallel to the principal axis.
An incident ray striking the mirror vertex has a reflected ray symmetric to the incident ray about the principal axis.
An incident ray parallel to the principal axis retraces its original straight line after reflection.
An incident ray passing through the focus retraces its original straight line after reflection.
An incident ray passing through the center of curvature retraces its original straight line after reflection.
An incident ray striking the mirror vertex is reflected along a straight line through the center of curvature.
An incident ray parallel to the principal axis passes through the focus after reflection.

intent.task: Recognize together the four convenient ray types for spherical-mirror construction and their respective reflection correspondences, rather than splitting four definitions into four true-or-false questions.
intent.source_solution: The complete source solution was frozen before constructing the options. A ray through the center of curvature is incident along the local normal and retraces its original straight line after reflection. A paraxial ray through the focus is reflected parallel to the principal axis. A ray striking the vertex has the principal axis as the local normal, so the reflected and incident rays are symmetric about the principal axis. A paraxial incident ray parallel to the principal axis is reflected through the focus. In the paraxial imaging situation defined by the source, any two convenient rays from the same object point that can actually be reflected, do not coincide, and uniquely determine an intersection are sufficient to locate the image point. There is no reflection at a hole; rays must strike the effective reflecting surface. This does not extend to exact convergence of arbitrarily wide beams or other spherical-mirror cases not supplied.
intent.unit_reason: The original written task asks for an entire set of convenient rays. One native multiple question preserves the joint distinction between four incidence conditions and four reflection outcomes. Eight candidate correspondences present four correct rules and four reproducible erroneous derivations; they are not eight independent questions, and the question count is not dictated by printed lines. Actual reflecting-surface availability and two-ray location are tested in a separate complete-plan judgment.
limitations: Selecting correct correspondences cannot demonstrate unaided recall and writing of the four convenient rays and their reasons.
Independent drawing of a ray diagram is not assessed; the selected original task asks for convenient rays and does not explicitly require submitting a diagram.

The stem explicitly limits the model to a paraxial concave mirror and an actual reflecting surface. It does not claim exact convergence of arbitrarily wide beams or supply unobserved source-figure geometry.

rationales.derivation: A paraxial ray incident parallel to the axis passes through the focus after reflection. Tracing this path in reverse, a ray through the focus toward the mirror is reflected parallel to the principal axis; this also agrees with the selected focus-ray definition.

An incident line through the center of curvature is the normal at its contact point on the spherical surface and retraces the same straight line after reflection. For an off-axis object point, this line is not parallel to the principal axis, so the asserted parallel result does not follow.
rationales.misconception: Treat the center of curvature as the focus: first misread passing through the center of curvature as passing through the focus, then apply the focus-to-axis-parallel reflection rule.

rationales.derivation: The local normal at the mirror vertex is the principal axis. The reflection law makes the angles of incidence and reflection equal, so in the construction plane containing the principal axis, the incident and reflected rays are symmetric about it.

The axis-parallel ray from an off-axis object point strikes the spherical surface away from the axis, where its direction generally is not the local normal. Its paraxial reflected ray passes through the focus rather than retracing the incident straight line.
rationales.misconception: Treat the principal-axis normal at the vertex as a common normal for the entire curved surface. Because the incident ray is parallel to the principal axis, incorrectly classify incidence everywhere as normal and apply retracing at normal incidence.

rationales.derivation: Passing through the focus does not guarantee incidence along the normal at the spherical contact point. The paraxial reflected ray is parallel to the principal axis; the incident straight line from an off-axis object point to the focus is generally not that reflected straight line.
rationales.misconception: Mistake the focus for the center of curvature, treat a focus-crossing ray as normally incident, and apply the center-of-curvature ray retracing rule.

rationales.derivation: The straight line from a point on the spherical surface to its center of curvature is the local normal. A ray through the center of curvature is normally incident, so both angles are zero and the reflected ray retraces the original straight line in the opposite direction.

The line from the vertex to the center of curvature is the principal axis. The stipulated ray from an off-axis object point to the vertex makes a nonzero angle with this axis and retains an equal angle after reflection, rather than automatically traveling along the normal.
rationales.misconception: Correctly find that the vertex normal passes through the center of curvature, but identify all reflected rays with that normal. Discard the equal-angle constraint and incorrectly obtain a reflected ray along the center-of-curvature line.

rationales.derivation: Within the explicitly paraxial concave-mirror model, the focus is the point through which rays incident parallel to the axis pass after reflection, so the reflected ray passes through it. This is not generalized to exact convergence of arbitrarily wide beams.

view.stem: In a paraxial concave-mirror real-image construction, the mirror has a small central hole. A ray from an off-axis object point toward the mirror vertex passes through the hole. The other three convenient rays, through the center of curvature, through the focus, and parallel to the principal axis, all strike the effective reflecting surface, and their reflected paths are pairwise noncoincident. Which plan can locate this object point's image using actual reflected rays?

options.text: All three remaining reflected rays must be used together to locate their common intersection; any two reflected rays are insufficient to locate the image point.
Use the reflected ray of the vertex ray that passes through the hole together with any remaining reflected ray; still apply the vertex-reflection rule at the hole.
Choose any two of the three remaining reflected rays and locate the image point at their intersection; do not treat the ray through the hole as a reflected ray.
Use only one of the remaining reflected rays as the location constraint; the image point can be uniquely located along that ray.

intent.task: Judge a complete two-ray location plan constrained by the availability of an actual reflecting surface; distinguish two sufficient rays, a nonessential third ray, an underdetermined single ray, and nonexistent reflection at a hole.
intent.source_solution: The source solution was frozen before the options: a center-of-curvature ray retraces its path, a focus ray is reflected parallel to the principal axis, a vertex ray is symmetric about the principal axis, and an axis-parallel ray is reflected through the focus. These rules are limited to the seed's paraxial concave-mirror imaging range. Two actual reflectable, noncoincident convenient rays from the same object point locate its image at their reflected-ray intersection in this real-image model; a third ray is only a check, not compulsory. The central hole supplies no reflected ray, so two rays reflected by the remaining effective surface should be chosen instead. A single reflected straight line gives only a locus of positions and cannot select a unique image point on its own.
intent.unit_reason: This judges the sufficiency and actual availability of two rays in the selected definition context, distinct from the other question recognition of four ray correspondences. One native single unit compares complete construction plans, avoiding fragmented true-or-false questions about whether a third ray is needed or whether the hole reflects. No fixed question quota is assumed.
limitations: Recognizing the correct plan does not demonstrate independently writing or drawing the complete two-ray construction.

The central hole, reflectability of the other three ray types, and noncoincident reflected lines are explicitly supplied situation conditions. They come from the definition availability principle, not geometric facts from an unseen source figure.
Judgment is restricted to the stated paraxial real-image construction model; no hole diameter, beam width, distance, or other unknown source-figure parameter is inferred.

rationales.derivation: Two noncoincident reflected straight lines from the same object point already uniquely locate its image in the stated real-image model. A third reflected ray can pass through the same point as a check, but this does not make two rays insufficient.
rationales.misconception: Mistake checking the common intersection with a third ray for a necessary condition for locating the image. First require all three rays, then incorrectly reject any already-sufficient pair.

rationales.derivation: The incident ray through the hole does not strike a reflecting surface, so it has no actual reflected ray at the vertex. This plan treats nonexistent reflection as a location constraint.
rationales.misconception: Apply the vertex-reflection rule merely because the incident line points toward the geometric vertex, ignoring that the vertex is a hole rather than a reflecting surface. Draw a fictitious reflected line and intersect it with another line.

rationales.derivation: All three other convenient rays are actually reflected and have noncoincident reflected paths. The paraxial real-image model makes these rays from the same object point pass through the same image point, so any two uniquely locate it by intersection; reflection of the ray through the hole need not be assumed.

A single reflected straight line contains many possible positions and supplies no second independent location constraint. Ordinary ray construction requires another noncoincident reflected line to intersect it.
rationales.misconception: Mistake the direction constraint along one ray for a complete position constraint, claiming a unique image point on the line before there is an intersection with a second path.
